senses.d: Any insect of the order Diptera; characterized by having two wings (except for some wingless species), also called true flies.
Especially, any of the insects of the family Muscidae, such as the common housefly (other families of Diptera include mosquitoes and midges).
Those or any similar but not closely related insect, such as a dragonfly, butterfly, or gallfly.
A lightweight fishing lure resembling an insect.
ex: I went on trying for fish along the western bank down the river, but only small trout rose at my flies, and a score was the total catch.

senses.d: A chest exercise performed by moving extended arms from the sides to in front of the chest. (also flye)
The butterfly stroke (plural is normally flys).

ex: a trifling fly, none of your great familiars

senses.d: A parasite.
ex: The fly that plays too near the flame burns in it.

senses.d: A simple dance in which the hands are shaken in the air, popular in the 1960s.
A butterfly (combination of four options).
To travel through the air, another gas, or a vacuum, without being in contact with a grounded surface.
ex: Birds of passage fly to warmer regions as it gets colder in winter.
The probe flew beyond the solar system.

senses.d: To take a flight on a plane; to pilot or crew a plane.
ex: My airline needs me to get clearance before I can fly again.
If we want to fly today, we need to leave for the airport right now.

senses.d: To be in the winged adult stage.
ex: This species flies from late summer until frost.

senses.d: To be accepted, come about or work out.
ex: Let's see if that idea flies.
You know, I just don't think that's going to fly. Why don't you spend your time on something better?

senses.d: To cause to fly (travel or float in the air): to transport via air or the like.
ex: Charles Lindbergh flew his airplane The Spirit of St. Louis across the Atlantic ocean.
Birds fly their prey to their nest to feed it to their young.

senses.d: To arrange for someone to take a flight.
ex: We flew the kids out to see their grandparents.

senses.d: To pilot a plane over a region or on a route.
ex: This is the first time I flew the Pacific.
I'm hoping to fly the London-New York route so I can see the Big Apple again.

senses.d: To complete (a goal, task, mission, etc.) while crewing an aircraft or spacecraft.
To hunt with a hawk.

senses.d: To wave or flutter; to cause to wave or flutter.
ex: When the wind picked up, her hair flew back behind her head.
In her dance, she holds her hands above her head to fly those colorful ribbons in the air.

senses.d: The action of flying; flight.
An act of flying.
ex: There was a good wind, so I decided to give the kite a fly.

senses.d: A fly ball.

ety.text: From Middle English fleynge, fleeʒinge, flihinde, vlyinde, vleoinde, flyand, ffleghand, flighand (also fleoninde, fleonninde, etc.), from Old English flēogende, from Proto-Germanic *fleugandz (“flying”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”), equivalent to fly + -ing. Cognate with Saterland Frisian fljoogend (“flying”), West Frisian fleanend (“flying”), Dutch vliegend (“flying”), German Low German flegend (“flying”), German fliegend (“flying”), Danish flyvende (“flying”), Swedish flygande (“flying”), Icelandic fljúgandi (“flying”).

From Middle English flyinge, fleyng, fleyinge, fleynge, fleghyng, fleiʒeyng, flyeghynge, equivalent to fly + -ing. Cognate with Danish flyvning (“flying”), Swedish flygning (“flying”), Norwegian flyvning, flygning, flyging, flying (“flying”).
